title: The Hymn of Cold Spring
premise: Elodie Voss, a pest controller who has spent a lifetime refusing to believe in anything she can't trap or poison, is hired to clear Cold Spring House of an infestation that leaves fingerprints in the dust — too large, too many joints, and always arranged like hands pressed against glass from the inside. The house's heir, Marcus Thorne, sleeps through everything while old recordings of his grandmother's lullaby play on loop; when Elodie's own monitoring equipment captures a second voice answering questions no one asked aloud, he is dragged into the house's inheritance: a song sung each generation to keep something fed beneath the spring, and a family that has always paid its singer in years of life. Marcus must learn the hymn's final verse — the verse that ends the bargain rather than renewing it — without singing along before the first frost completes its pattern across every window and door. He learns it, nearly loses himself to the melody, and at the climax sings it alone as the frost closes in, breaking the pact but inheriting the thing's attention; the ending leaves him alive, marked, and teaching Elodie the first line so he will never have to carry the song by himself again.
about_author: Hazel Thackeray is the pen name of a former archivist who spent six years cataloguing estate sales in rural Vermont, where she collected more lullabies than invoices. She writes horror about houses that remember their owners, and insists she has never once hummed while working.

chapters.title: Fingerprints in the Flour
chapters.summary: Elodie Voss takes a routine call to Cold Spring House, expecting mice, and finds handprints in the pantry dust — oversized, many-jointed, pressed outward as if from behind the wall. His skeptical POV establishes the voice: nothing exists until it's trapped, tagged, or billed. Emotional beat: professional irritation masking a flicker of unease he refuses to name.

chapters.title: The Heir Who Sleeps
chapters.summary: Marcus Thorne, the house's exhausted young heir, hires Elodie for a full season, admitting the infestation predates him and that his grandmother 'handled it' before. Marcus's POV reveals his guilt over selling off the estate and his chronic, unnatural sleepiness after sundown. Beat: two men circling the same secret, neither willing to say it first.

chapters.title: Bait That Won't Take
chapters.summary: Elodie sets traps throughout the house; by morning they're sprung, empty, and rearranged into a neat spiral on the kitchen table. His POV documents the evidence with photographs he tells himself are lighting artifacts. Beat: the first crack in his disbelief — not fear yet, just the insult of being mocked by something with better manners than his clients.

chapters.title: Recordings After Midnight
chapters.summary: Elodie installs audio monitors to track movement overnight. The recordings capture footsteps, then humming — a slow, minor-key lullaby matching the sheet music framed in the hallway. Marcus's POV: he recognizes the tune as his grandmother's, the one she forbade him to sing past the second verse. Beat: dread arriving through nostalgia.

chapters.title: A Second Voice
chapters.summary: Reviewing the tapes, Elodie hears the lullaby stop mid-phrase — and a low voice answer, asking questions in an older dialect of English. The questions are addressed to the sleeping house. His POV frays as he realizes the voice pauses, expectantly, whenever Marcus stirs. Beat: skepticism becomes obsession; he replays the tape forty times.

chapters.title: The Spring Beneath the Floor
chapters.summary: Following a cold draft, Elodie finds a sealed hatch above the original spring that named the town, its water black and perfectly still, ringed by generations of scratched tally marks. Marcus's POV, woken by Elodie's shouting, remembers being told never to look down the well as a child. Beat: the house's true architecture revealed — built around the wound, not despite it.

chapters.title: Grandmother's Ledger
chapters.summary: In the attic, Marcus finds his grandmother's ledger: dates, verses sung, and payments received — decades added to her life in exchange for each renewal of the song. His POV confronts the corruption at the heart of his inheritance: she lived to ninety-four on borrowed time while the thing below grew patient and hungry. Beat: grief curdling into anger at the dead.

chapters.title: What the Voice Wants
chapters.summary: Elodie sets a live microphone at the hatch and asks the voice a question directly. It answers: it wants the verse finished, the bargain renewed, a Thorne to sing. When Elodie refuses, the temperature in the room drops and his breath frosts in July. His POV: terror finally arrives, and with it a terrible clarity. Beat: belief, unwanted and total.

chapters.title: Sleepwalking Toward the Well
chapters.summary: Marcus begins sleepwalking, found at dawn standing barefoot over the hatch, lips moving in the lullaby's rhythm. Elodie chains the door and stays awake watching him, recording. Marcus's POV drifts between dreams of his grandmother singing and waking horror at his own hands' chalk-pale skin. Beat: love and duty begin pulling in opposite directions.

chapters.title: The Neighbors Remember
chapters.summary: Elodie canvasses the village and finds the pattern: every fifty years a Thorne renews the song, and every fifty years the winter that follows is gentle while the singers' neighbors sicken. An old woman tells him the last holdout froze in June. His POV weighs warning the town against protecting Marcus. Beat: the horror widens beyond one house.

chapters.title: Verse by Verse
chapters.summary: Working from the ledger and the recordings, Elodie transcribes the hymn — three complete verses and a fourth that trails into scratches. He tests singing the first alone; the spring answers within seconds, delighted. Marcus's POV wakes to find Elodie hoarse and gray-faced, having bought information with his own breath. Beat: partnership forged in shared danger.

chapters.title: The Frost Writes First
chapters.summary: Frost patterns appear on the interior windows in July, spelling branching lines that match the tally marks around the well — a countdown. Elodie calculates the deadline: first frost, roughly five weeks. Marcus's POV feels the house pulling him toward sleep earlier each evening. Beat: the clock becomes visible, and merciless.

chapters.title: Duty's Inheritance
chapters.summary: Marcus's estranged father arrives, healthy at seventy and knowing exactly what the house is, demanding Marcus sing the renewal as every heir must. His POV exposes the family's machinery: power hoarded through the pact, passed down like a title. Beat: Marcus sees his future in his father's unlined face and recoils.

chapters.title: The Fourth Verse Exists
chapters.summary: Elodie traces the hymn to a hymnal fragment in the county archive: a fourth verse, struck through by a nineteenth-century hand, annotated 'the unbinding.' The archive copy is incomplete — three words missing. His POV races the frost and his own growing compulsion to hum. Beat: hope with a hole in it.

chapters.title: Seduction of the Song
chapters.summary: The voice changes tactics, speaking to Elodie directly now, offering him what it offered the Thornes: years, certainty, the end of doubt. He catches himself writing the missing words in a trance, unsure if they're recovered or dictated. Marcus's POV watches the man he's come to rely on slip toward the melody. Beat: corruption reaches outside the bloodline.

chapters.title: Father's Bargain
chapters.summary: Marcus's father attempts the renewal himself, singing at the hatch to cut his son out — and the thing below takes the payment differently, aging him decades in minutes and leaving him raving about the cold underneath everything. Marcus's POV holds his dying father and understands the price was never fair. Beat: duty dies with the father who weaponized it.

chapters.title: The Missing Words
chapters.summary: Cross-referencing his trance-writing against the archive fragment and the grandmother's marginalia, Elodie reconstructs the fourth verse — and realizes the final line requires a name freely given, not inherited. His POV confesses the trance to Marcus, surrendering control. Beat: trust as the counter-spell to the song's seduction.

chapters.title: Night Before Frost
chapters.summary: The forecast confirms frost by morning. Elodie and Marcus seal the upstairs rooms, burn the ledger pages the voice keeps whispering through, and sit together through the long dark while the lullaby plays itself on every device in the house. Alternating POV. Beat: quiet before catastrophe, tenderness sharpening the stakes.

chapters.title: The Singing
chapters.summary: At dawn the frost completes its pattern and the hatch opens on its own. Marcus descends to the spring and begins the hymn, Elodie anchoring him by reading the fourth verse aloud — spoken, never sung, so the melody cannot claim him. Climax: the voice rises to meet Marcus's, trying to turn the unbinding into a duet. Beat: love against duty made literal.

chapters.title: Last Verse, First Silence
chapters.summary: At the final line Marcus gives his own name freely — breaking the inheritance clause — and the spring goes silent mid-note. The frost retreats from the glass like a tide reversing. But the silence has weight, and both men feel the attention of something vast redirect toward them. Beat: victory shadowed by cost.

chapters.title: After the Thaw
chapters.summary: Weeks later: the house is warm, the traps stay empty, and Marcus's father is buried. Elodie packs his equipment but doesn't leave; the recordings still catch, once a night, a single held breath beneath the floor — listening, waiting, patient. His POV admits some things aren't ended, only renegotiated. Beat: uneasy peace.

chapters.title: Teaching the First Line
chapters.summary: On the porch of Cold Spring House, Marcus teaches Elodie the hymn's opening verse — not to sing, but to know, so the song will never again depend on one throat, one bloodline, one believer. Elodie, who has never believed, learns it anyway. Final beat: inheritance transformed from burden into shared vigil, and love chosen over duty's script.
